title: No Wife, No Funeral, No Feast
summary: God forbids Jeremiah to marry or have children, to enter a house of mourning, or to join a wedding feast, because the coming disaster will make all three meaningless. When the people ask what they have done wrong, Jeremiah is to name their idolatry and stubbornness. Yet in the middle of the judgment comes a promise of a new exodus from the north, and the chapter ends with the nations coming from the ends of the earth to confess that their fathers inherited only lies.
story: Jeremiah has already acted out one sign with a loincloth (chapter 13). Now his whole life becomes a sign. His unmarried state, his absence from funerals, and his absence from weddings all tell Judah what is coming: a time when families will be cut off, the dead will lie unburied, and the sounds of celebration will stop. The chapter carries forward the theme of the confessions (Jeremiah's isolation in 15:17) and gives it a reason. But it also looks past the exile. Verses 14 and 15 announce that the return from Babylon will be so great that it will replace the exodus from Egypt as the event by which Israel swears, a promise that reappears in 23:7-8 and shapes the hope of the second half of the book.
historical:
The chapter is undated, but it belongs to the years when Jeremiah was proclaiming the coming Babylonian conquest, probably during the reign of Jehoiakim (609 to 598 BC). The judgments it describes, including mass death from disease and famine, unburied bodies, and deportation to "a land that neither you nor your fathers have known", came to pass in the sieges of Jerusalem and the deportations of 597 and 586 BC. The "land of the north" in verse 15 is Babylon, whose armies entered Judah from the north even though Babylon itself lay to the east across the desert.

The promise of return was fulfilled in part after Cyrus of Persia conquered Babylon in 539 BC and allowed exiled peoples, including the Jews, to go home (Ezra 1). Jewish communities remained scattered across many lands for centuries afterward, which is one reason later Jewish and Christian readers continued to look for a fuller fulfillment of the gathering described here.
cultural:
Marriage and children were the ordinary expectation for an Israelite man, the way a family's name and land were carried on. Jeremiah's state would have been conspicuous and puzzling in a small town. That is exactly the point: people would ask why, and his answer was the message.

Mourning customs in verses 5 to 7 were public and communal. Neighbors came to lament, and a meal was shared in the house of the bereaved, with bread broken and "a cup of consolation" given to the mourners. The word for the funeral meal in verse 5 (marzeach) names a gathering known from other ancient texts, including texts from Ugarit on the Syrian coast, where it describes a kind of association that met for feasting, sometimes in connection with the dead. Amos uses the same word for the lavish banquets of Samaria's elite (Amos 6:7). Cutting oneself and shaving the head for the dead (verse 6) were widespread mourning rites in the ancient Near East, forbidden to Israel in the law (Leviticus 19:28; Deuteronomy 14:1) but evidently still practiced. The picture of fishermen and hunters (verse 16) would have been clear to anyone who had seen nets drawn in or game driven out of rocky hiding places: there will be no escape.
literary: The chapter falls into prose instructions and a closing poem. Verses 1 to 9 are three prohibitions (do not marry, do not mourn, do not feast), each followed by its explanation. Verses 10 to 13 use a question-and-answer form common in Jeremiah and Deuteronomy, in which the people ask why disaster has come and receive a reason. Verses 14 and 15 interrupt with sudden hope, introduced by the prophetic formula "the days are coming". Verses 16 to 18 return to judgment with the image of fishermen and hunters. Verses 19 to 21 are a short psalm of trust in which Jeremiah addresses God as his strength, fortress, and refuge, followed by God's answer. The phrase "the voices of the bride and bridegroom" (verse 9) is a refrain of the book (7:34; 25:10), and its return in 33:11 marks the reversal of this chapter's judgment.

outline.t: Do not marry or have children in this place
Do not enter a house of mourning
Do not enter a house of feasting
A new exodus from the land of the north
Fishermen and hunters: no hiding place
The nations will come and confess

doctrines.note: The removal of God's "peace", "loving devotion", and "compassion" (verse 5) shows that judgment is, at its heart, God withdrawing the gifts that made life good. The disasters are what life looks like when that protection is lifted.
Verses 14 and 15 promise a new exodus greater than the first. Even in the chapter of Jeremiah's loneliest calling, God speaks of bringing his people home.

The nations will come "from the ends of the earth" and renounce their idols (verse 19). The judgment on Israel is part of a larger purpose in which all peoples come to know that God's name is the LORD.
Marriage and children are a good gift, which is why forbidding them to Jeremiah is so severe a sign. The chapter treats family life as precious and shows how deeply judgment tears it apart.

words.note: Marzeach, translated here as "a funeral meal". Outside the Bible it names a banquet or a society that met to feast, sometimes connected with honoring the dead. In Amos 6:7 it describes the revelry of the idle rich. Here Jeremiah is barred from it: he cannot share the community's grief any more than its joy.

Chesed, loyal love, kindness, faithfulness to a covenant bond. The BSB translates it "loving devotion". It is one of the richest words in the Old Testament, describing God's steady commitment to his people. For God to say he has removed his chesed from this people is to say the relationship has reached its breaking point, though elsewhere Jeremiah insists that God's chesed will finally prevail (31:3; 33:11).

Dayyag, a fisherman. In verse 16 God will send many fishermen to catch his people, an image of being hunted down for judgment, not gathered for rescue. The picture recalls Amos 4:2, where people are dragged away with fishhooks.

christ: The promise of a new exodus in verses 14 and 15 is one of several in the prophets (compare Isaiah 43:16-19), and the New Testament presents the work of Jesus as that greater exodus: Luke even describes his coming death as his departure, using the Greek word exodos (Luke 9:31). Jesus' call to his first disciples to become fishers of men (Mark 1:17) uses the same kind of image as verse 16, though in Jeremiah the fishermen gather for judgment and in the Gospel for rescue; whether Jesus meant to echo this verse is uncertain. Verse 19, with the nations streaming to God from the ends of the earth, anticipates the gospel going to all peoples. And Jeremiah's lonely, single life as a sign of a coming crisis has a thematic parallel in Paul's advice about singleness in view of the present distress (1 Corinthians 7:26), and in Jesus' own life lived wholly for the kingdom.

hard.q: Why would God forbid Jeremiah to marry, have children, or comfort the grieving?
hard.a: These commands deprived Jeremiah of the ordinary goods of life, and they were meant to be seen. His empty house and his absence from funerals and weddings were a living sermon: soon families would be destroyed, mourning would be impossible, and joy would fall silent. Some readers also see mercy in the first command, since any wife and children Jeremiah had would have faced the horrors of the siege described in verses 3 and 4. The prohibition on mourning did not mean God no longer cared about grief; the same God weeps over his people elsewhere in the book (9:1; 14:17). It dramatized that the coming disaster would be so vast that the normal rituals of comfort would collapse. The command was for Jeremiah in his time, and nothing in the text makes it a rule for others, but it shows that a calling can cost a person the things everyone else takes for granted.

questions: Jeremiah's ordinary life became a message to his neighbors. What does your way of living say, without words, about what you believe?
God says the return from exile will be greater than the exodus. Where have you seen God do something new that surpassed an earlier rescue?
Verse 20 asks, "Can man make gods for himself?" What gods do people make for themselves today, and why do they keep making them?
